claims.source: After only 15 min of conditioning, they undergo active demethylation (F(1,82) = 63.8, p<0.0001, N vs. C15 min) that does not occur following pseudoconditioning trials of randomly unpaired stimuli (F(1,82) = 0.15, p=0.70, N vs. Ps).
claims.evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Demethylation of CG sites does not occur following pseudoconditioning trials of randomly unpaired stimuli.
claims.source: After only 15 min of conditioning, they undergo active demethylation (F(1,82) = 63.8, p<0.0001, N vs. C15 min) that does not occur following pseudoconditioning trials of randomly unpaired stimuli (F(1,82) = 0.15, p=0.70, N vs. Ps).
claims.evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Selected CA sites in the tBDNF coding sequence are either methylated in naïve and demethylated after conditioning or methylated after conditioning.
claims.source: We also observed that there are selected CA sites in the coding sequence that are either methylated in naïve and demethylated after conditioning (e.g., site 26, p=0.002) or methylated after conditioning (Figure 2A, lower panel, e.g., sites 27, 39, 40, 46, p<0.01).
claims.evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: CA sites in the tBDNF coding region undergo active conditioning-dependent methylation/demethylation in only 15 min.
claims.source: Therefore, in addition to CG dinucleotides, CA sites in the coding region also undergo active conditioning-dependent methylation/demethylation in only 15 min.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the bisulfite sequencing data showing changes in CA methylation.

claims.claim: Splicing of the tBDNF2a transcript was significantly inhibited after zebularine or RG108 application compared to naïve and pseudoconditioned preparations.
claims.source: Splicing of the tBDNF2a transcript was significantly inhibited after zebularine or RG108 application compared to naïve and pseudoconditioned preparations (Fig. 2B, F(3,16) = 80.0, n = 5/group, p<0.01).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Demethylation has a causative role in cessation of splicing of the tBDNF2a transcript.
claims.source: These data indicate a strong mechanistic role for demethylation in the cessation of splicing.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the DNMT inhibitor experiments showing that induced demethylation suppresses splicing.

claims.claim: ChIP-qPCR showed strong binding of total MeCP2 protein to tBDNF in the naïve state corresponding with splicing of the tBDNF2a transcript.
claims.source: ChIP-qPCR showed strong binding of total MeCP2 protein to tBDNF in the naïve state corresponding with splicing of the tBDNF2a transcript (Figure 2C, 2aON).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: MeCP2 binding to tBDNF was observed in the region surveyed by primer set P1 which is upstream of the actual splice site.
claims.source: This was observed in the region surveyed by primer set P1 which is, interestingly, upstream of the actual splice site.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data using primer set P1.

claims.claim: With conditioning when the coding sequence undergoes rapid demethylation, ChIP indicates a significant reduction in MeCP2 binding to just 4% of naïve.
claims.source: With conditioning when the coding sequence undergoes rapid demethylation, ChIP indicates a significant reduction in MeCP2 binding to just 4% of naïve (Figure 2C, n = 5/group, p<0.0001, N vs. C15 min) that corresponds with cessation of splicing and suppression of the tBDNF2a transcript (2aOFF).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: During conditioning, MeCP2 was observed to increase binding in the region surveyed by primer set P2.
claims.source: During this time, MeCP2 was also observed to increase binding in the region surveyed by primer set P2 (Figure 2C, p=0.07) suggesting that it may be translocated to this downstream site rather than vacating genomic DNA entirely.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Levels of total MeCP2 protein were unchanged during conditioning.
claims.source: These alterations in binding occurred even though levels of total MeCP2 protein were unchanged during conditioning (Figure 2D; n = 4/group, p=0.50).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: MeCP2 binding to tBDNF was significantly reduced in naïve preparations exposed to MeCP2 siRNA to 35% of normal naïve levels.
claims.source: Finally, ChIP-qPCR verified that MeCP2 binding was significantly reduced in naïve preparations exposed to MeCP2 siRNA to 35% of normal naïve levels (Figure 2C, p<0.001, N vs. siRNA) corresponding well with the 40% reduction in the tBDNF2a transcript after MeCP2 siRNA (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The tBDNF protein coding sequence is rapidly demethylated during conditioning resulting in reduced MeCP2 binding upstream of the splice site that corresponds with suppression of the alternatively spliced truncated tBDNF2a transcript.
claims.source: These findings indicate that the tBDNF protein coding sequence is rapidly demethylated during conditioning resulting in reduced MeCP2 binding upstream of the splice site that corresponds with suppression of the alternatively spliced truncated tBDNF2a transcript.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined BSP, ChIP, and RT-PCR data.

claims.claim: Co-immunoprecipitations show a strong interaction of total MeCP2 protein with YB-1 in both naïve and conditioned preparations that was not altered by conditioning.
claims.source: The results show a strong interaction of total MeCP2 protein with YB-1 in both naïve and conditioned preparations that was not altered by conditioning (Figure 3A, n = 3/group, p=0.91).
claims.evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The MeCP2-YB-1 association requires the presence of RNA.
claims.source: Additionally, we confirmed that the MeCP2-YB-1 association required the presence of RNA. Treatment of samples with DNaseI did not affect the co-IPs whereas treatment with RNase A inhibited it (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by co-IP data with DNase and RNase treatment shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: YB-1 was bound to the tBDNF coding region surveyed by primer set P1 in naïve preparations and was significantly reduced after conditioning.
claims.source: Like MeCP2, ChIP indicated that YB-1 was bound to this region in naïve preparations and was significantly reduced after conditioning (Figure 3C, n = 5/group, p=0.02).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The overall level of YB-1 protein was not altered after 15 min of conditioning compared to naive.
claims.source: Importantly, western blot data showed that the overall level of YB-1 protein was not altered after 15 min of conditioning compared to naive (n = 3/group, p=0.82).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data.

claims.claim: YB-1 binds to the same region of the coding sequence as MeCP2 during splicing and is similarly released in conditioning when it is suppressed.
claims.source: These results indicate that YB-1 binds to the same region of the coding sequence as MeCP2 during splicing and is similarly released in conditioning when it is suppressed.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP data showing parallel binding patterns for MeCP2 and YB-1.

claims.claim: Tet1 is bound to the tBDNF coding sequence in naïve and dissociates after conditioning.
claims.source: ChIP-qPCR showed that Tet1 is bound to the coding sequence in naïve and dissociates after conditioning (Figure 3C, p<0.001, N vs. C15 min).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: MeCP2, YB-1 and Tet1 are bound to a region upstream of the splice site in naïve preparations during splicing of the truncated tBDNF2a transcript and all three dissociate during conditioning when splicing stops.
claims.source: Taken together, the ChIP data show that MeCP2, YB-1 and Tet1 are bound to a region upstream of the splice site in naïve preparations during splicing of the truncated tBDNF2a transcript and all three dissociate during conditioning when splicing stops.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined ChIP data for all three proteins.

claims.claim: Release of MeCP2, YB-1, and Tet1 binding during conditioning corresponds with significantly increased levels of H3K4me3 in the same region of the coding sequence.
claims.source: Interestingly, release of binding during conditioning corresponds with changes in histone modifications in the same region of the coding sequence that consists of significantly increased levels of H3K4me3 (Figure 3C, p=0.01) and reduced H3K27me3 (p<0.01, N vs. C15 min), alterations that would lead to a more permissive, or open, chromatin structure.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Release of MeCP2, YB-1, and Tet1 binding during conditioning corresponds with reduced H3K27me3 in the same region of the coding sequence.
claims.source: Interestingly, release of binding during conditioning corresponds with changes in histone modifications in the same region of the coding sequence that consists of significantly increased levels of H3K4me3 (Figure 3C, p=0.01) and reduced H3K27me3 (p<0.01, N vs. C15 min), alterations that would lead to a more permissive, or open, chromatin structure.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Bath application of YB-1 siRNA to naïve preparations resulted in a significant 53% knockdown of YB-1 protein expression compared to normal naïve.
claims.source: Bath application of the siRNA to naïve preparations resulted in a significant 53% knockdown of YB-1 protein expression compared to normal naïve (Figure 3D, n = 3/group, p<0.01).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Analysis of mRNA transcripts in naïve preparations treated with YB-1 siRNA showed that expression of spliced tBDNF2a was reduced to 42% of its normal naïve values.
claims.source: Significantly, analysis of mRNA transcripts in naïve preparations treated with YB-1 siRNA showed that expression of spliced tBDNF2a was reduced to 42% of its normal naïve values (Figure 3E, n = 5/group; p=0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Expression of the other three exon II transcripts (tBDNF2b-d) were not significantly affected by YB-1 siRNA treatment.
claims.source: These findings were specific to the 2a transcript as expression of the other three exon II transcripts were not significantly affected by YB-1 siRNA treatment (tBDNF2b-d, F(1,28) = 0.10, p=0.75).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data.

claims.claim: Tet1 siRNA applied to naïve nearly completely suppressed the tBDNF2a transcript to only 4% of normal naïve values.
claims.source: These data are replotted here and show that Tet1 siRNA applied to naïve nearly completely suppressed the tBDNF2a transcript to only 4% of normal naïve values (Figure 3E, p=0.0003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3E and cited from a previous study.

claims.claim: YB-1 and Tet1 are key partners with MeCP2 that are required for alternative splicing of the tBDNF2a transcript.
claims.source: Therefore, YB-1 and Tet1 are key partners with MeCP2 that are required for alternative splicing of the tBDNF2a transcript.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the siRNA experiments showing that knockdown of either YB-1 or Tet1 inhibits splicing.

claims.claim: YB-1 ChIP was significantly inhibited from binding in naïve preparations treated with MeCP2 siRNA.
claims.source: Assessment of YB-1 ChIP revealed that it was significantly inhibited from binding in naïve preparations treated with MeCP2 siRNA (Figure 3C, p=0.01, N vs. siRNA) as would be expected if MeCP2 recruits YB-1.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The MeCP2 siRNA did not alter the overall level of YB-1 protein compared to normal naïve.
claims.source: Because MeCP2 also has a transcriptional function, control experiments were performed showing that the MeCP2 siRNA did not alter the overall level of YB-1 protein compared to normal naïve (n = 3/group, p=0.66).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data.

claims.claim: Tet1 ChIP was significantly reduced by application of MeCP2 siRNA to naïve preparations.
claims.source: Importantly, we also observed that Tet1 ChIP was significantly reduced by application of MeCP2 siRNA to naïve preparations (Figure 3C, p=0.02, N vs. siRNA).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Protein levels of Tet1 were unaffected by MeCP2 siRNA treatment.
claims.source: This occurred even though protein levels of Tet1 were also unaffected by the treatment (n = 3/group, p=0.57).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data.

claims.claim: The histone modifications H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 showed significantly reduced ChIP signals following MeCP2 siRNA treatment.
claims.source: Further follow-up of these results indicated that the histone modifications analyzed here, H3K4me3 associated with active genes and H3K27me3 associated with repressed genes, showed significantly reduced ChIP signals following MeCP2 siRNA treatment (Figure 3C, H3K4me3, p=0.001; H3K27me3, p<0.01, N vs. siRNA) suggesting that MeCP2 also exerts control over chromatin structure.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: MeCP2 exerts control over chromatin structure.
claims.source: Further follow-up of these results indicated that the histone modifications analyzed here, H3K4me3 associated with active genes and H3K27me3 associated with repressed genes, showed significantly reduced ChIP signals following MeCP2 siRNA treatment (Figure 3C, H3K4me3, p=0.001; H3K27me3, p<0.01, N vs. siRNA) suggesting that MeCP2 also exerts control over chromatin structure.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the histone modification ChIP data after MeCP2 knockdown.

claims.claim: Conditioning-induced demethylation was significantly inhibited following conditioning in MeCP2 siRNA as shown for individual CG sites in the coding sequence.
claims.source: Our results further show that this was significantly inhibited following conditioning in MeCP2 siRNA as shown for individual CG sites in the coding sequence (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by BSP data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: There was an overall reduction in conditioning-induced demethylation across the coding sequence with MeCP2 siRNA treatment during conditioning compared to normal conditioning.
claims.source: Grouped data show there was an overall reduction in conditioning-induced demethylation across the coding sequence with MeCP2 siRNA treatment during conditioning compared to normal conditioning (Figure 4B, left panel, p<0.0001, C15 min vs. C15 MeCP2 siRNA).
claims.evidence: This is supported by BSP data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Inhibition of Tet1 tBDNF binding by MeCP2 siRNA treatment severely attenuates the demethylation process that normally takes place during conditioning.
claims.source: Therefore, inhibition of Tet1 tBDNF binding by MeCP2 siRNA treatment severely attenuates the demethylation process that normally takes place during conditioning.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined ChIP and BSP data showing reduced Tet1 binding and reduced demethylation after MeCP2 siRNA.

claims.claim: Levels of 5hmC were high in the tBDNF coding regions surveyed by primer sets P1 and P2 in naïve preparations.
claims.source: Our results showed that levels of 5hmC were high in the coding regions surveyed by primer sets P1 and P2 in naïve preparations (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by MeDIP data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: After conditioning, values for 5hmC MeDIP were substantially reduced in all three primer set regions.
claims.source: After conditioning, values for 5hmC MeDIP were substantially reduced in all three primer set regions (Figure 4D, n = 5/group, F(5,29) = 58.2, p=0.001, N vs. C15 min), presumably reflecting conversion by Tet-mediated iterative oxidation to unmethylated C (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by MeDIP data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Treatment of naïve preparations with MeCP2 siRNA that inhibited Tet1 tBDNF binding resulted in a significant reduction in 5hmC.
claims.source: Moreover, treatment of naïve preparations with MeCP2 siRNA that inhibited Tet1 tBDNF binding also resulted in a significant reduction in 5hmC (Fig. 4D, F(5,29) = 33.4, p=0.001, N vs. N MeCP2 siRNA) consistent with Tet1's role in establishing this epigenetic mark.
claims.evidence: This is supported by MeDIP data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: In conditions in which Tet1 function is compromised by MeCP2 siRNA, 5mC predominates in the naïve state in place of 5hmC.
claims.source: These findings suggest that in conditions in which Tet1 function is compromised by MeCP2 siRNA, 5mC predominates in the naïve state in place of 5hmC (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined MeDIP and BSP data.

claims.claim: Analysis of the methylation status of the coding sequence after Tet1 siRNA application by BSP showed that it remained highly methylated similar to untreated naïve preparations.
claims.source: Analysis of the methylation status of the coding sequence after Tet1 siRNA application by BSP showed that it remained highly methylated similar to untreated naïve preparations (Figure 5A, p=0.17).
claims.evidence: This is supported by BSP data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Levels of 5hmC were nearly doubled after Tet1 siRNA treatment compared to normal naïve.
claims.source: Further analysis by MeDIP demonstrated that levels of 5hmC were nearly doubled after Tet1 siRNA treatment compared to normal naïve (Figure 5B, p=0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by MeDIP data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Binding of MeCP2 and YB-1 to the tBDNF coding sequence was significantly inhibited after Tet1 siRNA treatment.
claims.source: Surprisingly, binding of MeCP2 and YB-1 to the tBDNF coding sequence was significantly inhibited (Figure 5C, n = 5/group, MeCP2, p<0.01, YB-1, p<0.01), which accounts for the suppression of splicing in Tet1 siRNA treated naïve preparations.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Tet3 binding to tBDNF was greatly increased after Tet1 siRNA treatment.
claims.source: These data showed minimal binding in normal naïve preparations that was greatly increased after Tet1 siRNA treatment (Figure 5C, n = 3/group, p=0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The enhanced binding of Tet3 after Tet1 siRNA was not accompanied by any changes in protein expression.
claims.source: The enhanced binding of Tet3 was not accompanied by any changes in protein expression (Ambigapathy et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The MeCP2-YB-1 complex was not recruited to methylated DNA under conditions in which there is loss of Tet1, which is replaced by Tet3.
claims.source: These ChIP data indicate that the MeCP2-YB-1 complex was not recruited to methylated DNA under conditions in which there is loss of Tet1, which is replaced by Tet3.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP data showing reduced MeCP2-YB-1 binding and increased Tet3 binding after Tet1 siRNA.

claims.claim: CTCF binding is modified by DNA methylation such that it is evicted by 5mC to control exon splicing in the lymphocyte CD45 model gene.
claims.source: CTCF binding is also modified by DNA methylation such that it is evicted by 5mC to control exon splicing in the lymphocyte CD45 model gene (Shukla et al., 2011; Marina et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Expression of the CTCF protein was significantly increased to 168% over naïve values during conditioning.
claims.source: Expression of the CTCF protein was observed to be regulated during conditioning as it was significantly increased to 168% over naïve values (Figure 6B, n = 5/group, p=0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The CTCF siRNA resulted in a reduction in protein expression to 27% of normal naïve preparations.
claims.source: The siRNA was designed against conserved CTCF sequences in the turtle (nt 1187–1212) that resulted in a reduction in protein expression to 27% of normal naïve preparations (Figure 6C, lower left panel, n = 3/group, p=0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Application of CTCF siRNA to naïve preparations failed to have any effect on tBDNF2a splicing.
claims.source: Application of the siRNA to naïve preparations failed to have any effect on tBDNF2a splicing, as shown by the semi-quantitative data (Figure 6C, lower right panel, n = 5/group, p=0.91, N vs. N CTCF siRNA).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: When conditioned preparations that normally suppress splicing were treated with CTCF siRNA, the tBDNF2a transcript was unmasked and splicing resumed at levels similar to normal naïve preparations.
claims.source: Interestingly, however, when conditioned preparations that normally suppress splicing were treated with CTCF siRNA, the tBDNF2a transcript was unmasked and splicing resumed at levels similar to normal naïve preparations (Figure 6C, p<0.0001, C15 vs. C15 CTCF siRNA).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: CTCF insulates DNA sequences from the splicing apparatus during normal conditioning thereby suppressing the truncated tBDNF2a transcript.
claims.source: These data provide compelling evidence that CTCF insulates DNA sequences from the splicing apparatus during normal conditioning thereby suppressing the truncated tBDNF2a transcript.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the CTCF siRNA experiments showing that CTCF knockdown during conditioning restores splicing.

claims.claim: ChIP assays of CTCF binding to the coding region showed significantly increased signals within primer sets P1 and P3 during conditioning.
claims.source: To provide additional support for our interpretation of splicing insulation, ChIP assays of CTCF binding to the coding region showed significantly increased signals within primer sets P1 and P3 during conditioning (Figure 6D, n = 5/group; P1: p=0.002; P3, p<0.05, N vs. C15 min).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: There was strong CTCF binding to region P2 that was not conditioning-dependent.
claims.source: While there was strong binding to region P2 this was not conditioning-dependent (Figure 6D, p=0.12).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Analysis with ChIP for RNAPIISer2 showed no significant conditioning-related changes in binding to the coding exon.
claims.source: Analysis with ChIP for RNAPIISer2 showed no significant conditioning-related changes in binding to the coding exon (Figure 6E, n = 5/group; F(5,24) = 1.40, p=0.26) suggesting that CTCF does not affect binding of the elongating form of RNAPII.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: CTCF does not affect binding of the elongating form of RNAPII.
claims.source: Analysis with ChIP for RNAPIISer2 showed no significant conditioning-related changes in binding to the coding exon (Figure 6E, n = 5/group; F(5,24) = 1.40, p=0.26) suggesting that CTCF does not affect binding of the elongating form of RNAPII.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the RNAPIISer2 ChIP data showing no changes during conditioning.

claims.claim: Depletion of MeCP2 by siRNA results in a significant reduction in CTCF ChIP of both naïve and conditioned preparations compared to untreated preparations.
claims.source: The results showed a significant reduction in CTCF ChIP of both naïve and conditioned preparations treated by MeCP2 siRNA compared to untreated preparations (Figure 6D, N siRNA P1: p=0.01, C15 siRNA P1: p<0.0001; N siRNA P2: p<0.001, C15 siRNA P2: p<0.001) even though overall protein levels were unaffected by the treatment (Figure 6F, n = 3/group, p=0.44).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 6D and western blot data shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: Overall CTCF protein levels were unaffected by MeCP2 siRNA treatment.
claims.source: The results showed a significant reduction in CTCF ChIP of both naïve and conditioned preparations treated by MeCP2 siRNA compared to untreated preparations (Figure 6D, N siRNA P1: p=0.01, C15 siRNA P1: p<0.0001; N siRNA P2: p<0.001, C15 siRNA P2: p<0.001) even though overall protein levels were unaffected by the treatment (Figure 6F, n = 3/group, p=0.44).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: The loss of Tet1 binding in MeCP2-treated preparations resulted in a functionally significant elevation in 5mC in the tBDNF coding sequence that would normally undergo conversion to unmethylated C during conditioning.
claims.source: The loss of Tet1 binding in MeCP2-treated preparations resulted in a functionally significant elevation in 5mC in the tBDNF coding sequence that would normally undergo conversion to unmethylated C during conditioning.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined ChIP and BSP data showing reduced Tet1 binding and elevated methylation after MeCP2 siRNA.

claims.claim: The change in methylation status after MeCP2 siRNA was accompanied by inhibition of CTCF binding during conditioning that can be attributed to its eviction by abnormally high levels of 5mC.
claims.source: This change in methylation status was accompanied by inhibition of CTCF binding during conditioning that can be attributed, based on the work of others, to its eviction by abnormally high levels of 5mC.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined methylation and ChIP data, and supported by citations to previous work on CTCF and methylation.

claims.claim: In MeCP2 null male mice, dynamically modified, but not stable, 5hmC loci were found to be significantly reduced compared to controls.
claims.source: Interestingly, in MeCP2 null male mice, dynamically modified, but not stable, 5hmC loci were found to be significantly reduced compared to controls (Szulwach et al., 2011), consistent with our findings.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Depletion of MeCP2 protein may alter DNA methylation status indirectly by preventing binding of other DNA modifying proteins, including Tet.
claims.source: Taken together, available evidence suggests that depletion of MeCP2 protein may alter DNA methylation status indirectly by preventing binding of other DNA modifying proteins, including Tet.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that MeCP2 knockdown reduces Tet1 binding and affects methylation patterns.

claims.claim: MeCP2 and Tet1 are binding partners.
claims.source: Evidence indicates that MeCP2 and Tet1 are binding partners (Cartron et al., 2013; Ambigapathy et al., 2015) but the functional impact of this relationship has been largely unstudied.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: MeCP2 and Tet1 together may regulate the overall content of 5mC and 5hmC for dynamically modulated genes.
claims.source: It is possible that MeCP2 and Tet1 together regulate the overall content of 5mC and 5hmC for dynamically modulated genes.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed interactions between MeCP2 and Tet1.

claims.claim: Loss of MeCP2 destabilizes the regulatory process for control of DNA methylation across the genome.
claims.source: Loss of MeCP2 destabilizes this regulatory process for control of DNA methylation across the genome.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing altered methylation patterns after MeCP2 knockdown.

claims.claim: MeCP2 is a global regulator of chromatin structure and may serve as an integral component of the chromatin architecture itself.
claims.source: An alternative but not mutually exclusive mechanism relates to the view that MeCP2 is a global regulator of chromatin structure and may serve as an integral component of the chromatin architecture itself (Skene et al., 2010; Cohen et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Inhibition of MeCP2 severely depleted the tBDNF coding sequence of the histone modifications H3K4me3 and H3K27me3.
claims.source: In our study, we observed that inhibition of MeCP2 severely depleted the tBDNF coding sequence of the histone modifications H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 that have a significant role in regulating gene expression.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data showing reduced histone modifications after MeCP2 siRNA.

claims.claim: Loss of MeCP2 may affect learning-related tBDNF binding by regulatory proteins, including Tet1, through its action on controlling the accessibility of the surrounding chromatin structure.
claims.source: Therefore, loss of MeCP2 may affect learning-related tBDNF binding by regulatory proteins, including Tet1, through its action on controlling the accessibility of the surrounding chromatin structure.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on histone modifications and protein binding after MeCP2 knockdown.

claims.claim: Increased chromatin compaction observed in MeCP2-null neurons in vivo might restrict activity-dependent DNA regulatory mechanisms leading to a disruption in gene methylation and expression.
claims.source: Along these lines, increased chromatin compaction observed in MeCP2-null neurons in vivo might restrict activity-dependent DNA regulatory mechanisms leading to a disruption in gene methylation and expression (Linhoff et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study and inferred from the current findings.

claims.claim: The human BDNF gene codes for antisense BDNF transcripts that may additionally regulate transcript expression.
claims.source: Notably, the human BDNF gene also codes for antisense BDNF transcripts that may additionally regulate transcript expression (Liu et al., 2005; Pruunsild et al., 2007) that may not be present in rat or mouse (Aid et al., 2007), although this is debatable (Modarresi et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Internal splicing, although rare, has been documented in other genes from normal human and patient populations or rodents.
claims.source: Although the intraexonic splicing event described here in turtle is an unconventional one, internal splicing, although rare, has been documented in other genes from normal human and patient populations (Cox et al., 2001; Tran et al., 2006; Madrigal et al., 2016) or rodents (Ye et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The truncated BDNF protein in turtle has a pattern of expression opposite to mature BDNF protein during conditioning.
claims.source: While the functional significance of the spliced transcript in turtle BDNF is unknown, it generates a truncated protein that has a pattern of expression opposite to mature BDNF protein during conditioning (Ambigapathy et al., 2013), suggesting it may have a dominant negative function.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claims.claim: The truncated BDNF protein may have a dominant negative function.
claims.source: While the functional significance of the spliced transcript in turtle BDNF is unknown, it generates a truncated protein that has a pattern of expression opposite to mature BDNF protein during conditioning (Ambigapathy et al., 2013), suggesting it may have a dominant negative function.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed expression pattern.

claims.claim: Mechanisms regulating splicing, such as Tet-mediated DNA methylation and control of MeCP2-YB-1 and CTCF binding, are highly conserved and consistent with previous studies in mammals.
claims.source: Our evidence indicates that mechanisms regulating splicing, such as Tet-mediated DNA methylation and control of MeCP2-YB-1 and CTCF binding, are highly conserved and consistent with previous studies in mammals (Young et al., 2005; Shukla et al., 2011; Maunakea et al., 2013; Marina et al., 2016).

results.result: An intraexonic splicing event in the turtle BDNF gene generates a truncated tBDNF2a transcript in naïve brain that is rapidly and completely suppressed during classical conditioning. This 40 bp deletion produces a frameshift and unique C-terminal end, and the suppression is stimulus-specific.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C3, C31-C32, and C50-C58 collectively demonstrate the existence and conditioning-dependent regulation of the tBDNF2a transcript through RT-PCR, sequencing, and quantitative analysis (Figures 1C-E). The data show clear bands at 185 bp (spliced) and 225 bp (unspliced) in cDNA but only 225 bp in genomic DNA, confirming intraexonic splicing. Quantitative data show tBDNF2a is suppressed to 8% of naïve values after 15 min conditioning (n=5, p=0.001), providing strong statistical support.

results.result: MeCP2 is instrumental for splicing of the tBDNF2a transcript. MeCP2 siRNA knockdown (to 59% of normal levels) results in substantial inhibition of tBDNF2a to about 40% of naïve values, while other tBDNF transcripts (2b-d) are not affected.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C59-C62 are well-supported by siRNA knockdown experiments with appropriate controls (Figures 1D-G). Western blots confirm MeCP2 protein reduction (n=4, p<0.001), RT-PCR shows selective reduction of tBDNF2a (n=5, p=0.001), and scrambled siRNA controls show no effect. The selectivity for tBDNF2a over other transcripts (2b-d) supports a splicing-specific rather than transcriptional mechanism.

results.result: The tBDNF coding sequence undergoes rapid, conditioning-dependent demethylation at CG and CA sites within 15 minutes. This demethylation is stimulus-specific (not occurring with pseudoconditioning) and has a causative role in cessation of splicing, as demonstrated by DNMT inhibitor experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C69 are supported by bisulfite sequencing data (Figure 2A) showing significant demethylation of CG sites (F(1,82)=63.8, p<0.0001) and specific CA sites after conditioning but not pseudoconditioning. DNMT inhibitor experiments (zebularine, RG108) that induce demethylation also suppress splicing (Figure 2B, F(3,16)=80.0, p<0.01), establishing causality. Sample sizes (3×7-10 clones/group) are adequate for BSP analysis.

results.result: MeCP2 binds to methylated tBDNF chromatin upstream of the splice site in naïve preparations and dissociates during conditioning when demethylation occurs. MeCP2 binding is reduced to 4% of naïve levels during conditioning, corresponding with cessation of splicing, while total MeCP2 protein levels remain unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6, C36-C38, and C70-C76 are supported by ChIP-qPCR data (Figure 2C) showing strong MeCP2 binding in naïve that is significantly reduced during conditioning (n=5, p<0.0001). Western blots confirm unchanged total MeCP2 protein levels (n=4, p=0.50), indicating redistribution rather than degradation. The correlation between MeCP2 siRNA-induced reduction in binding (to 35%) and transcript reduction (to 40%) provides additional support for the functional relationship.

results.result: YB-1 is a functional partner of MeCP2 required for tBDNF2a splicing. YB-1 interacts with MeCP2 in an RNA-dependent manner, binds to the same tBDNF region as MeCP2, and dissociates during conditioning. YB-1 knockdown reduces tBDNF2a to 42% of naïve values without affecting other transcripts.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C81, C86-C88, and C90 are supported by co-IP experiments (Figure 3A-B) showing MeCP2-YB-1 interaction that requires RNA (RNase sensitive, DNase insensitive), ChIP data showing parallel binding patterns (Figure 3C, n=5, p=0.02), and YB-1 siRNA experiments (Figure 3D-E) with 53% knockdown (n=3, p<0.01) resulting in selective reduction of tBDNF2a (n=5, p=0.001). The specificity for tBDNF2a supports a splicing mechanism.

results.result: Tet1 binds to the tBDNF coding sequence in naïve preparations alongside MeCP2 and YB-1, dissociates during conditioning, and is required for splicing. Tet1 siRNA nearly completely suppresses tBDNF2a to 4% of naïve values.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83, C89-C90 are supported by ChIP data (Figure 3C) showing Tet1 binding in naïve that dissociates during conditioning (p<0.001), and Tet1 siRNA experiments (Figure 3E) showing dramatic suppression of tBDNF2a (p=0.0003). The magnitude of the effect (96% reduction) demonstrates Tet1 is essential for splicing. Sample sizes are adequate (n=5 for ChIP, n=5 for RT-PCR).

results.result: MeCP2 knockdown inhibits binding of YB-1 and Tet1 to tBDNF without affecting their protein expression levels, and also reduces histone modifications H3K4me3 and H3K27me3, suggesting MeCP2 controls chromatin structure and recruits these splicing-related proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C91-C96 are supported by ChIP data (Figure 3C) showing reduced YB-1 (p=0.01) and Tet1 (p=0.02) binding after MeCP2 siRNA, with western blots confirming unchanged protein levels (n=3, p=0.66 for YB-1, p=0.57 for Tet1). Histone modification ChIP shows reduced H3K4me3 (p=0.001) and H3K27me3 (p<0.01). This demonstrates MeCP2's role in recruiting partners and controlling chromatin accessibility.

results.result: MeCP2 knockdown negatively impacts DNA methylation dynamics during conditioning by inhibiting Tet1 binding, resulting in attenuated demethylation and reduced 5hmC levels. In naïve MeCP2 siRNA-treated preparations, 5mC predominates in place of 5hmC.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C97-C99, and C100-C103 are supported by BSP data (Figure 4A-B) showing significantly reduced conditioning-induced demethylation after MeCP2 siRNA (p<0.0001), and MeDIP data (Figure 4D) showing high 5hmC in naïve that is reduced after conditioning (F(5,29)=58.2, p=0.001) and after MeCP2 siRNA treatment (F(5,29)=33.4, p=0.001). Sample sizes are adequate (3×10 clones for BSP, n=5 for MeDIP). The data support the interpretation that MeCP2 loss impairs Tet1 function.

results.result: Tet1 and MeCP2 are critical functional partners for splicing regulation. Tet1 knockdown results in high methylation, nearly doubled 5hmC levels, compensatory Tet3 binding, but paradoxically reduced MeCP2-YB-1 binding and suppressed splicing, demonstrating reciprocal functional dependence.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C109, C150-C153 are supported by BSP (Figure 5A, p=0.17 vs naïve), MeDIP (Figure 5B, p=0.001), and ChIP data (Figure 5C) showing reduced MeCP2 and YB-1 binding (n=5, p<0.01) but increased Tet3 binding (n=3, p=0.001) after Tet1 siRNA. The paradoxical finding that high methylation with Tet1 loss reduces MeCP2 binding suggests Tet1-mediated 5hmC is required for MeCP2 recruitment, supporting their functional partnership. The data are internally consistent and well-controlled.

results.result: CTCF binds to demethylated tBDNF chromatin during conditioning and suppresses splicing through an insulator mechanism. CTCF protein expression increases to 168% during conditioning, CTCF siRNA has no effect in naïve but restores splicing during conditioning, and ChIP shows increased CTCF binding at regions P1 and P3.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C40-C41, and C111-C117 are supported by western blots (Figure 6B, n=5, p=0.001), CTCF siRNA experiments (Figure 6C) showing restoration of splicing during conditioning (p<0.0001) but no effect in naïve (p=0.91), and ChIP data (Figure 6D) showing increased binding at P1 (p=0.002) and P3 (p<0.05). The siRNA rescue experiment provides strong evidence for CTCF's role in suppressing splicing during conditioning. Sample sizes are adequate.

results.result: MeCP2 knockdown inhibits CTCF binding to tBDNF during conditioning without affecting CTCF protein levels. This occurs because MeCP2 loss impairs Tet1-mediated demethylation, resulting in elevated 5mC that evicts CTCF from its binding sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C118-C123 are supported by ChIP data (Figure 6D) showing reduced CTCF binding after MeCP2 siRNA in both naïve and conditioned preparations (p=0.01 to p<0.0001), western blots showing unchanged CTCF protein (Figure 6F, n=3, p=0.44), and RNAPIISer2 ChIP showing no changes (Figure 6E, F(5,24)=1.40, p=0.26). The mechanistic interpretation linking MeCP2 loss → reduced Tet1 binding → elevated 5mC → CTCF eviction is well-supported by the combined data from Figures 4 and 6.

results.result: Mutations in MECP2 can have secondary effects on DNA methylation and alternative splicing by preventing binding of DNA modifying proteins including Tet1, resulting in aberrant binding by regulatory proteins and altered splicing patterns, destabilizing methylation control across the genome.
results.evaluation: Claims C14, C42-C44, C125, and C128 represent the major conclusion synthesized from the experimental data. The evidence from MeCP2 siRNA experiments showing reduced Tet1 binding (C93), altered methylation patterns (C97-C98), reduced CTCF binding (C120), and altered splicing (C60) collectively support this conclusion. This is a well-justified inference from the experimental results, though it extrapolates from the specific tBDNF example to broader genomic implications.

results.result: The deficits caused by MeCP2 loss of function are exposed in a physiological learning-dependent context (conditioning) and not under steady state conditions, as demonstrated by the differential effects of MeCP2 siRNA on splicing regulation during conditioning versus naïve states.
results.evaluation: Claim C45 is supported by the experimental design showing that MeCP2 siRNA effects on methylation and CTCF binding are most pronounced during conditioning (Figures 4A-B, 6D). The data show that MeCP2 siRNA in naïve reduces splicing but the full impact on methylation dynamics and CTCF binding is revealed during conditioning. This represents an important conceptual advance showing activity-dependent MeCP2 functions.

results.result: Release of MeCP2, YB-1, and Tet1 binding during conditioning corresponds with increased H3K4me3 and reduced H3K27me3 in the tBDNF coding sequence, alterations that would lead to a more permissive chromatin structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 are supported by ChIP data (Figure 3C) showing increased H3K4me3 (p=0.01) and reduced H3K27me3 (p<0.01) during conditioning when MeCP2, YB-1, and Tet1 dissociate. The interpretation that these changes create more open chromatin is reasonable based on established histone code principles. Sample size is adequate (n=5).

results.result: MeCP2 knockdown negatively impacts conditioning-dependent splicing regulation, as shown by altered responses to conditioning in MeCP2 siRNA-treated preparations.
results.evaluation: Claim C13 is supported by data showing that MeCP2 siRNA affects the normal conditioning-dependent suppression of splicing through its effects on Tet1 binding, methylation dynamics, and CTCF binding (Figures 4, 6). This is a summary claim well-supported by the detailed mechanistic data.

results.result: Suppression of tBDNF2a splicing is stimulus-specific, being inhibited by paired but not unpaired nerve stimulation, and not by general increases in neuronal excitability evoked by glutamate or high potassium.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35 are supported by citations to the authors' previous work (Ambigapathy et al., 2013). While not directly demonstrated in this manuscript, the pseudoconditioning controls (Figure 2A) showing no demethylation with unpaired stimuli provide supporting evidence. This establishes the specificity of the conditioning paradigm.

results.result: The MeCP2 binding site (P1 region) is upstream from the splice site (P3 region), and chromatin looping is proposed to bring these regions into close proximity for functional interaction.
results.evaluation: Claim C143 is supported by ChIP data showing binding at different locations (Figure 2A, 6D). However, claim C144 proposing chromatin looping is speculative and not directly tested. While the model is reasonable and consistent with CTCF/cohesin function, no chromosome conformation capture (3C, 4C, Hi-C) or similar experiments were performed to demonstrate looping. The 374 bp distance between P1 and P3 (C166) raises questions about whether looping is necessary or even likely at such short range.

results.result: Preliminary findings show no MeCP2-Tet3 interaction, and it is speculated that Tet3 does not recruit MeCP2 or may even repel it, explaining why MeCP2 binding is reduced when Tet1 is replaced by Tet3.
results.evaluation: Claim C154 is based on preliminary unpublished data, and claim C155 is explicitly speculative. While the observation that Tet3 replacement correlates with reduced MeCP2 binding (C106, C150) is well-supported, the mechanistic interpretation lacks direct experimental evidence. Co-IP experiments with Tet3 would be needed to test this hypothesis.

results.result: The two CTCF binding sites at P1 and P3 may reflect paired CTCF/cohesin interactions required for loop formation that protects the splice site, though it is uncertain whether such short-range loops (374 bp) can occur or be mediated by CTCF/cohesin.
results.evaluation: Claims C165 and C167 are speculative. While CTCF binding at two sites is demonstrated (C116, C164), the loop formation model is not tested experimentally. The authors appropriately acknowledge uncertainty about whether 374 bp loops can form or be mediated by CTCF/cohesin. This would require chromosome conformation capture experiments to resolve.

results.result: CTCF may have dual functions in regulating alternative splicing, through RNAPII pausing to promote splicing or by its insulator function to inhibit splicing.
results.evaluation: Claim C162 is speculative reasoning based on the current findings and previous literature. The data show CTCF suppresses tBDNF2a splicing without affecting RNAPIISer2 binding (C118-C119), which argues against the RNAPII pausing mechanism in this case. The dual function hypothesis is plausible but not directly tested here.

results.result: MeCP2 and Tet1 together may regulate the overall content of 5mC and 5hmC for dynamically modulated genes.
results.evaluation: Claim C127 is speculative reasoning based on the observed interactions. While the data show MeCP2 and Tet1 affect each other's function at tBDNF (C151-C152), extrapolation to genome-wide regulation of dynamically modulated genes requires additional evidence. This is a reasonable hypothesis for future testing but not directly demonstrated.

results.result: The truncated BDNF protein may have a dominant negative function based on its opposite pattern of expression compared to mature BDNF during conditioning.
results.evaluation: Claim C136 is speculative, based on expression patterns from previous work (C135). While the opposite expression pattern is suggestive, no functional experiments testing dominant negative activity are presented. Protein-protein interaction studies, functional assays, or rescue experiments would be needed to support this hypothesis.

results.result: Background and literature context establishing that: (1) Rett syndrome is caused by MECP2 mutations leading to widespread gene misregulation; (2) MeCP2 binds methylated DNA and hydroxymethylated DNA; (3) MeCP2 partners with splicing factors including YB-1; (4) alternative splicing is ubiquitous and important in brain; (5) BDNF gene structure and function; (6) CTCF binding is methylation-sensitive and involved in splicing regulation.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1, C15-C30, C46-C49, C110, C124, C126, C129, C133-C134, C137-C142, C146-C149, C156-C157, C160-C161, C163, C168-C170) represent established knowledge from the literature, supported by appropriate citations. They provide necessary context for interpreting the experimental findings. The citations appear appropriate and the claims are consistent with current understanding in the field.

results.result: Inhibition of MeCP2 severely depletes the tBDNF coding sequence of histone modifications H3K4me3 and H3K27me3, suggesting MeCP2 controls chromatin structure and may affect learning-related tBDNF binding by regulatory proteins through controlling chromatin accessibility. This is consistent with increased chromatin compaction in MeCP2-null neurons restricting activity-dependent mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C132 are supported by ChIP data (Figure 3C) showing reduced H3K4me3 (p=0.001) and H3K27me3 (p<0.01) after MeCP2 siRNA. The interpretation about chromatin structure control is reasonable and supported by citation to previous work (C132). This provides a plausible alternative or complementary mechanism to direct protein recruitment for how MeCP2 loss affects Tet1 and other protein binding.

results.result: The downregulation of full-length tBDNF transcripts (2b-d) during conditioning is mediated by enhanced methylation of the exon II promoter and binding by transcriptional repressor BHLHB2, not by the splicing mechanism affecting tBDNF2a.
results.evaluation: Claim C145 is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Ambigapathy et al., 2015) and is consistent with the current data showing that MeCP2 siRNA selectively affects tBDNF2a but not 2b-d (C62). This distinguishes transcriptional from post-transcriptional regulation mechanisms.
